notes.meaning: Ezekiel receives a new message from God. It likely came after Jerusalem had been destroyed, when people were asking why it happened. From here on, Ezekiel's message turns mostly to comfort and promise.

The "shepherds" are Israel's leaders, especially the kings and rulers, and some older writers include priests and prophets too. A shepherd's job is to care for the sheep. These leaders cared only for themselves. The picture fits, since King David was taken from tending sheep to lead God's people.

The leaders took the best of everything: the fat (or milk), the wool, the finest sheep. They squeezed the people with heavy taxes. They even had wealthy people killed so they could seize their property, as King Ahab did to Naboth. Living off the flock is not wrong in itself, but they gave nothing back.

Here is the list of what a good shepherd should do: strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bandage the hurt, bring back the wanderers, and search for the lost. These leaders did none of it. Instead they ruled harshly, the way Pharaoh treated the Israelites as slaves in Egypt. God's law had forbidden ruling like that.

With no real shepherd, the people scattered and fell prey to enemy nations, pictured as wild beasts. The leaders still had the title of shepherd, but they did not do the work. Jesus later grieved over crowds who were "like sheep without a shepherd" (Matthew 9:36).

God calls them "My flock." They still belong to Him, even though the leaders treated them as their own property. The people were scattered far and wide, and no one bothered to look for them. The hills were also where idols were worshiped, with the rulers' approval.

God calls the shepherds to listen and swears by His own life. He repeats the charge: His sheep became prey because the shepherds fed themselves instead of the flock. Those who would not listen to God's directions must now hear His sentence.

God says He is against these shepherds. He will hold them responsible for every missing sheep and remove them from their job. The leaders had been feeding on the flock like wild animals. God will rescue His sheep from their mouths. Those who lead God's people will one day give an account to Him (Hebrews 13:17).

The LORD Himself will now do what the bad shepherds failed to do. He will search for His sheep, because they are His. Every promise that follows grows out of this one: God Himself will be the Shepherd. Jesus later takes up this picture when He calls Himself the Good Shepherd (John 10).

God will look for His people the way a caring shepherd hunts for scattered sheep. The "day of clouds and darkness" means the time of the nation's disaster and distress. It looks ahead to Jesus' story of the shepherd who goes after the one lost sheep (Luke 15). This promise comforts God's people in every dark time.

God promises to gather His scattered people from the nations and bring them home to their land. This first came true when many Jews returned from Babylon. It also pictures Christ gathering His people to Himself.

differ.view: The homecoming is picture-language for God gathering His wandering people back to Himself in the Church.
Besides the return from Babylon, this points to a literal, worldwide return of the Jewish people to the land of Israel.

notes.meaning: God will lead His flock to rich, green pasture on Israel's mountains, like Psalm 23. For the returning exiles this meant the land's good food and also worship at the temple again. For believers it pictures being fed by God's word and care.
God Himself will tend His flock and let them lie down. Lying down means real rest after tiring wandering, and a settled home. No one will drive them out or frighten them anymore.

God does point by point what the bad shepherds failed to do in verse 4. The "sleek and strong" are the rich and proud who bully the weak, and He will destroy them. He shepherds with justice, meaning fairness, not the cruelty of the old rulers. He has rest for troubled believers and a warning for proud sinners.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible, following ancient Greek and Latin versions, reads "that which was fat and strong I will preserve."

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translations, like the RSV, also follow those ancient versions and read "I will watch over" the fat and strong.

notes.meaning: Now God turns from the leaders to the people themselves. The flock contains different kinds of people, and He knows how to tell them apart. The "rams and goats" are the rich and powerful among ordinary people who copied the rulers by pushing the poor around. The leaders' sins do not excuse the flock's own sins.

The strong sheep eat the best grass and drink the clear water. Then they trample and muddy whatever is left, so the weaker sheep get only scraps. It is a picture of rich people who take more than they need and spoil the rest for the poor. Older writers also saw it as spoiling God's pure word and twisting justice before it reached ordinary people.
God Himself will judge between the fat sheep and the thin ones, meaning the rich who oppress and the humble poor. His judgment means He will stand up for the poor.

The strong shoved the weak aside with shoulders and horns until they were driven away. Adding pain to people already hurting is cruel. God promises to rescue His flock so they will no longer be prey. A small taste of this came after the return from Babylon, when the poor got some relief (Nehemiah 5). The full fulfillment was still to come.

God promises one shepherd, "My servant David." King David had died about four hundred years earlier, so this means a greater Son of David: the Messiah, Jesus. Jesus points back to this when He says, "I am the Good Shepherd" (John 10). He is "one" shepherd in place of many bad ones, uniting God's divided people into one flock.

differ.view: Take the name plainly: King David himself will be raised to rule Israel as a prince under Jesus in the Millennium, Christ's future thousand-year reign on earth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some later scholars think Ezekiel may mean a line of good rulers in David's spirit rather than one person, though others still judge a personal Messiah the safest reading.

notes.meaning: The LORD will be their God, and His servant David will be prince among them. "Servant" means this ruler does God's will, not his own, unlike the selfish kings. Jesus fully lived this out as the obedient Servant (Isaiah 42:1). Those who have Jesus as their Prince have the LORD as their God.

A covenant is a binding promise-relationship, and this one brings peace, meaning every good thing. God fulfills His old promise from Leviticus 26 to remove dangerous animals so His people can sleep safely even in the wild. Christians have also seen this as Christ defeating sin, Satan and death, so believers can rest without fear.

"My hill" is Zion, God's hill at Jerusalem. God will make His people and their land a blessing, and the blessing will reach others around them. Rain "in season" mattered greatly in Israel, where rain came only at set times. Christians have long prayed for these "showers of blessing" as the refreshing work of the Holy Spirit wherever Christ is preached.

Trees and fields will be fruitful, and God's people will be safe. God will break their yoke as He did in Egypt, freeing them from those who used them as slaves. Through this rescue they will truly know He is the LORD. Older Christian writers also saw freedom from sin and Satan here (Luke 1:74).

Enemy nations will no longer prey on God's people, and they will live in safety. God promises more than safety from harm. He also promises freedom from fear, so no one will frighten them. If God is for us, who can be against us?

Older Bibles say "plant of renown," while the BSB says "garden of renown." Many Christian writers saw the Messiah here, the "Branch" from David's family (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5). He feeds His people as the Bread of Life, so they will no longer starve or be mocked by other nations.
Through these blessings the people will know that God is with them, present and at peace with them. They will know they are His own people, bound to Him by the covenant made with their ancestors.

God seals the whole promise with tender words: you are My flock, My people, and I am your God. Older Bibles add "you are men," a reminder of how great it is that the holy God stoops to care for weak humans. If we take God as our God, He takes us as His people.
